This paper introduces the TVPAutoReg model, a novel method for forecasting multivariate count time series that explicitly models mutual dependencies and individual historical trends. We establish the theoretical statistical properties of TVPAutoReg, demonstrating that all parameters converge at optimal rates under relatively mild assumptions. Furthermore, we prove that the resulting in-sample forecasts are asymptotically efficient relative to a broad class of competing models. To evaluate the model's out-of-sample predictive performance, we introduce a simple yet effective metric and validate its utility across both simulated data and two real-world datasets. The analysis of these real data sets also yields actionable insights into the underlying characteristics of the series under study. Finally, to facilitate practical implementation, we develop a simple algorithm for selecting the optimal p-order in a SARIMA(p,0,0)(1,0,0)(1,0,0) configuration. Extensive numerical experiments confirm that the TVPAutoReg model significantly outperforms alternative approaches in terms of out-of-sample predictive performance. The proposed methodology is made available as an R package named tvpautoReg at https://github.com/chenyuxiang/R-tvpautoReg. Our results indicate that TVPAutoReg possesses strong predictive capabilities and can serve as a valuable tool for risk managers and other stakeholders in financial sectors, including insurance and banking. Additionally, the framework's flexibility makes it applicable to various fields such as epidemiology, sports analytics, and operations management. Potential theoretical and practical extensions of this work are also discussed.

The atmosphere contains a mixture of gases and particles that collectively cause light absorption and scattering, phenomena responsible for various sky visibility effects. While the role of gases in altering the direction of light is negligible, aerosols significantly scatter light, an effect that has historically been difficult to measure. Consequently, determining the optical properties of atmospheric aerosols has required an array of techniques, each with distinct advantages and limitations. These methods have been essential for developing climate models and supporting air quality management strategies. Over the past decade, there has been a surge in interest in deriving aerosol optical depths (AOD) from the residuals of extractions aimed at identifying the signatures of stellar variability in the amplitudes of photometric variations. This approach, known as the "stellar photometry method," has seen numerous applications and, more recently, a specialized technique has emerged to measure the Angström exponent from these same datasets. Despite its utility, the method has faced criticism regarding the accuracy of its AOD estimates. This perspective outlines recent efforts to address these challenges, highlighting a novel approach to improving AOD precision and a new method for detecting outliers in the data that may indicate errors in derived aerosol single scattering tendencies. Additionally, we describe a technique to estimate vertical inhomogeneities in AOD and discuss the potential for retrieving the complex refractive index and size distribution of aerosols from the resulting datasets. Although this workflow relies entirely on passive remote sensing, its final product aligns closely with the information obtainable through active lidar sensing, for which we also propose a simplified method to derive backscatter tendencies. Ultimately, this comprehensive dataset of atmospheric characteristics should facilitate significant advances in modeling radiative transfer and the development of operational inversion algorithms. We introduce a simple yet potent enhancement to the standard Euclidean Langevin dynamics sampler, designed to accelerate sampling for extensive configurational spaces in energy-based models. By integrating a "sturdy" integrator that utilizes an outer loop with a smaller time step within an inner loop step-size adaptation scheme, our approach ensures rapid convergence. Empirical comparisons across four large-scale molecular systems demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms conventional Langevin dynamics, achieving speedups of up to fifty-fold. Additionally, we validate the efficacy of the outer time step through experiments involving a highly flexible peptide, where the inner time step fixed at 0.002 was found to be nearly three times faster than the setup used in prior work. The implementation of this sampler is accessible at https://github.com/NeelamSrivastava/LELD.

Currently, no automatic system for generating image captions can fully leverage the vast collections of human-written references found in existing image-datasets. This paper proposes a framework that incorporates these references to evaluate how well automated descriptions align with human perspectives. Applying this framework to three public datasets—MSCOCO, VQA-ImageDescription, and its variant MSCOCO-VD—we observed that while existing automatic descriptions generally capture the main scene elements, they frequently miss crucial details present in the human references. Furthermore, these models often struggle with grammatical accuracy and fail to effectively integrate contextual information. We also analyzed the characteristics of the gaps between automatic and human descriptions, identifying specific sub-tasks where current methods fall short. To address these issues, we introduced a simple yet effective end-to-end neural network called Context-Embed-Net, which utilizes a two-stage training approach. Experimental results demonstrate that Context-Embed-Net significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple evaluation metrics. The source code and trained models for Context-Embed-Net will be made available at https://github.com/rajivkumar1994/Context-Embed-Net.

We present a simple, parametric prediction for the number of baryons and mesons produced per unit rapidity as a function of the center-of-mass energy $\sqrt{s}$ in hadronic collisions. This model integrates recent findings from hydrodynamics, which indicate that the baryon-to-strange quark ratio ($R_{B/S}$) scales with entropy density ($s$) as $s^{-1/3}$, and from thermal physics, which suggest that the $R_{B/S}$ follows a power law relative to temperature ($T$) across a broad range. By combining these principles with the scaling of entropy with energy in central collisions, we derive a power-law dependence of $R_{B/S}$ on $\sqrt{s}$. Consequently, the baryon yield per unit rapidity ($dN_B/dy$) scales as $(\log(s))^2$, while the meson yield ($dN_M/dy$) follows $(s)^{\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ represents the ratio of the power-law exponents governing $R_{B/S}$ versus $\sqrt{s}$. Utililing LHC and RHIC data, we determine that $\alpha \approx 0.12 \pm 0.01$, implying that baryon yields grow more slowly than meson yields with increasing energy. These predictions are potentially testable at future facilities such as the Fixed-Field Alternating Gradient (FFAG) collider, the Baryon Factory, and the High Energy Heavy Ion Collider (HEIC). Such measurements would provide valuable insights into the physics of ultra-high-energy cosmic air showers. Additionally, these scaling laws may have significant implications for predictions of particle yields in neutron star mergers and other astrophysical contexts. We conclude by outlining the potential applications of these yield predictions in various physical scenarios. This work serves as a companion to Reference 1, which offers a detailed derivation of the underlying assumptions and a comprehensive analysis of the results. Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) demands a methodology that integrates statistical analysis with rigorous theoretical considerations. While the specific theoretical choices—such as the selected factorization scale, matching scheme, and evolution equation—do not influence the underlying statistical fit, they directly affect the resulting PDFs and their uncertainties. Consequently, a unified framework capable of fitting PDFs across different schemes and orders is both advantageous and necessary. This document presents such a framework, detailing the necessary theoretical and statistical components. We offer a comprehensive overview of the involved theories, outlining their interconnections and the mathematical transformations required to convert between them. Furthermore, we describe the practical implementation, covering the conversion of data from various experiments and theoretical sources, the formulation of data vectors, and the construction of the covariance matrix. Finally, we examine the calculation of errors and confidence levels, providing a consistent approach for assessing uncertainties. The implementation of this framework within the TROID software is also discussed. Although designed for PDF fits, this framework is broadly applicable to any analysis involving data transformation and error evaluation, serving as a valuable tool for combining diverse datasets. We conclude by highlighting several potential use cases. The source file for this document is troid_source.tex, which utilizes the nosection class option to prevent automatic heading creation and the glossaries package for defining and listing terminology; access to this file is available at https://github.com/TROID-framework/Theory-framework-for-PDF-fitting-.tex. Key terms and definitions include: all-order, confidence-level, factorization-scale, Fitter, matching-scheme, parton-distribution-function, PDF, statistical-analysis, theory-framework, trivial-relation, uncertainty, and UUncertainty. This study employs a direct numerical simulation (DNS) to investigate how a turbulent jet fire responds to acoustic forcing within a linearized framework, aiming to enhance an active fire suppression technique known as the "flapping sleeve" (FLAPS). The simulation integrates large-eddy modeling of compressible gas flow with a one-step global reaction model. Acoustic waves are introduced via a monopole source through an active zone at the inlet, while the FLAPS method is simulated at the outlet using a moving boundary condition. To decouple the response measurements from the specific characteristics of the suppression source, a global mode decomposition (GMD) is applied to the velocity and heat release rate fluctuations along the inlet centerline. This decomposition yields a set of global modes and their corresponding frequencies, which are ranked by the energy contained in their axial velocity and heat release rate components. The results indicate that for Reynolds number $Re=10000$, the flame stabilizes in a V-shape with an oblique shock visible at the expansion section. Furthermore, two primary global modes were identified: a first mode exhibiting an axisymmetric acoustic standing wave with a heat release rate perturbation concentrated at the shock, and a second mode displaying a Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in the shear layer with heat release rate oscillations on both sides of this layer. These findings offer valuable insights for developing an optimal active fire suppression strategy. Ultimately, this research contributes to the understanding of vortex-shock and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities in compressible turbulent flows and provides an framework for characterizing these instabilities in the context of active fire suppression. Keywords: Direct numerical simulation (DNS), fire, global mode decomposition (GMD), FLAPS, active fire suppression, vortex-shock instability, Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, boundary condition. While multiple sets of tetrads and connections can be utilized to formulate the NLG model, these components do not possess unique definitions. Consequently, selecting specific constitutive elements is necessary to ensure the model remains practical, physically meaningful, and capable of generating novel, testable nonlocal predictions. This article reviews the theory of nonlocal gravity, emphasizing the interplay between tetrads and constitutive connections. The discussion begins with the geometric foundation of tetrads in both local and nonlocal contexts, followed by an analysis of how these fields interact with geodesic acceleration operators and the equation of motion within a local inertial frame. The review concludes with a detailed examination of the NLG model as applied to cosmic acceleration and gravitational waves. High-performance workloads demand fast CPU frequencies for optimal execution. However, existing CPUs operate below their maximum frequencies due to thermal and power constraints, creating a bottleneck that limits overall system performance. To address this, we introduce HyperDegrade, a technique that intentionally pushes CPU frequencies beyond their hardware limits to enhance performance for performance-critical workloads. By optimizing task scheduling and managing thermal constraints, HyperDegrade ensures that higher frequencies yield genuine performance gains. Our evaluations demonstrate that workloads running at frequencies 1.5 times lower than their peak can achieve performance improvements of up to 25% through HyperDegrade. Additionally, workloads already executing at or near their maximum frequency have been shown to gain an extra 17% performance. These results indicate that CPUs operating significantly below their optimal frequency can benefit from HyperDegrade, whereas those already close to their limit can see modest but meaningful enhancements. Furthermore, we provide guidelines for selecting the most effective frequency for HyperDegrade based on specific thermal headroom and workload characteristics. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first attempt at executing workloads at frequencies exceeding their nominal hardware capabilities. The open-source implementation of HyperDegrade is available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/HyperDegrade.

Colliding gravitational waves (CGWs) generate tidal accelerations that induce differential arm length changes in gravitational wave (GW) detectors. As these detectors rely on interferometric measurement, induced arm accelerations generate inertial acceleration noise (AN), which limits sensitivity when measuring CGWs. Additionally, as AN depends on arm length, current detectors like LIGO and Virgo face significant challenges with long arms when detecting high-frequency GWs. This paper introduces a new interferometric topology, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer (SS-I), which mitigates AN by approximately an order of magnitude at high frequencies through a topology-induced inertial effect. We anticipate that the SS-I will enhance GW detectability at high frequencies, and we expect the SS-I topology to be beneficial for future high-precision interferometric sensors beyond the GW community. The derivation of this inertial effect and the optimization of the SS-I topology are detailed in this paper. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of realizing the SS-I using existing GW detectors and other high-precision interferometric sensors, and we provide the design principles for applying the SS-I topology to future sensors. This study presents a system designed to identify and correct errors in OCR outputs when extracting vote totals from scanned election ballots. While deep learning-based end-to-end solutions exist for similar tasks, they demand extensive training datasets. Our approach leverages existing OCR systems, particularly those based on neural networks like Tesseract v5, which have already been trained on vast collections of printed text. By combining this with other techniques, we can derive significant benefits without the need for additional training data. Our method utilizes graph theory and voting-specific context to correct character recognition mistakes, offering a low-cost solution that can be adapted to any ballot type. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated using real-world vote counts extracted from scanned ballots across various elections and states. Results indicate that our method surpasses standard neural OCR systems by approximately 15% in accuracy when handling ballots with blurred, noisy, or distorted text. The source code and a demo are accessible at https://github.com/nathanrue/iOCR, while further details on the technique and its applications can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.09073. Ultimately, this tool serves as a practical utility for vote tabulation software, election analysts, auditors, and researchers working with historical ballot data.

We introduce a stochastic hydrodynamic formulation for interacting Bose gases, derived directly from the Beliaev-Leggett phase-space master equation. Through systematic expansions in both mass density and noise intensity, we recover deterministic Beliaev-Leggett hydrodynamics and identify a corresponding stochastic hydrodynamic equation. Unlike previous approaches, our method yields a closed equation that incorporates Beliaev-Leggett self-energies to account for thermal fluctuations, alongside noise terms responsible for anomalous diffusion. This stochastic hydrodynamic framework is then generalized to include superfluid effects via a Nelson-like approach, resulting in a comprehensive theory of stochastic superfluid hydrodynamics that integrates thermal fluctuations, Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer order, and related phenomena. Finally, we derive a random hydrodynamic version of the Beliaev-Leggett master equation and use it to derive Born-Markov approximations, ultimately constructing a closed set of deterministic hydrodynamic equations that go beyond the Beliaev-Leggett framework. As a practical application, we develop a random initial condition model capable of simulating thermal gases evolving under these advanced deterministic equations. Finally, we report on selected numerical experiments conducted within this framework.

Human beings possess the capacity to learn new tasks through guidance from other individuals, a capability that artificial intelligence systems lack. Knowledge graphs serve as a structured representation of world knowledge, linking entities via relationships, and can be constructed automatically from textual data or curated through interactions between humans and computers. The latter approach, known as active learning from text, has been a significant area of research for some time. Recently, there has been increased emphasis on educating humans about the existence, meanings, and appropriate usage of specific entities and relationships within a given knowledge graph. This shift has given rise to language education frameworks, which aim to refine corpus-based construction of subgraphs by incorporating human linguistic knowledge. Similarly, knowledge acquisition frameworks leverage a corpus to build or update a broader knowledge graph via structured interactions between a system and a human. These frameworks can be categorized into learner-pilot and educator-pupil frameworks; the former guides a human in teaching a corpus-based system, while the latter involves an expert educating a human, who then annotates a text for the knowledge graph. Despite their differences, both frameworks rely on a natural language-to-structure pipeline and have recently converged to create hybrid approaches. Education frameworks, in particular, offer unique insights into how humans organize knowledge, making them valuable for studying linguistic knowledge and its application in knowledge graphs and neural models. This survey examines various knowledge acquisition and education frameworks, focusing on educator-pupil and learner-pilot models, their corresponding interactions, and the underlying technologies. It also explores recent efforts to integrate these frameworks with neural methods, evaluates their performance, and identifies future research directions. Alongside this overview, we introduce a new classification system for knowledge acquisition frameworks based on the sources of knowledge they incorporate. Furthermore, we propose an innovative educator-pupil framework designed to teach a knowledge graph construction corpus about entity types and attributes, potentially expanding the representational capacity of such graphs.

This study introduces a novel, exact method for evaluating the null distribution of structured test statistics during the post-hoc analysis of ranked-data protocols, specifically for pairwise comparison tournaments. The proposed technique employs a specialized Markov chain that leverages the symmetries of the score vector to efficiently trace the data's transformation under the Fisher permutation test. We apply this method to two statistics: the classic linear Holm-Bonferroni (HB) correction and a new, potentially more powerful post-hoc correction termed "geometric-HB." Extensive simulations demonstrate that the geometric-HB/Holm approach yields higher statistical power than the traditional linear variant. Furthermore, we outline a practical implementation of this exact method within the R environment, making it accessible for real-world applications.

The sequence of anisotropic flow $v_n(p_t)$ as a function of transverse momentum serves as a primary indicator for characterizing the hydrodynamic behavior of the created medium in heavy ion collisions. In a non-central collision, the initial spatial anisotropy of the nucleon-nucleon overlap region is converted into momentum anisotropy by pressure gradients within the medium. Subsequently, the anisotropic flow of particles, particularly at higher $p_t$, is significantly influenced by partonic momentum broadening through parton scattering. Due to the geometric shape of the triangular nucleon-nucleon overlap in non-central events, $v_3}$ is expected to be the dominant anisotropic flow component. In central collisions, where the initial spatial eccentricity is nearly zero, $v_3}$ arises primarily from the intrinsic event-plane fluctuations of the nucleon-nucleon collision. This study examines the origins of $v_3}$ in both non-central and central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using a multi-phase transport model (AMPT). The results indicate that in the AMPT framework, $v_3}$ for central Au+Au collisions originates mainly from binary fluctuation, whereas for non-central events, it results from the combination of binary and shape anisotropy. Furthermore, the $v_3}$ generated by binary fluctuation in non-central Au+Au collisions accounts for approximately 70% of the total value. The anisotropic flow components $v_1$, $v_2$, and $v_3}$ produced in non-central AMPT simulations align well with experimental data from RHIC and LHC, supporting the validity of the model's mechanism for anisotropic flow in both central and non-central heavy ion collisions. This study presents a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter tailored for air traffic administration, incorporating a birth prior that models the non-parametric distribution of undetected points across multiple Bernoulli components. Unlike conventional approaches that use a histogram to represent the non-parametric distribution, this work introduces a novel birth model with partial grid orientation. This model defines the non-parametric distribution along one axis as a set of Dirac deltas, while describing it as an arbitrary density function along the remaining axis. Consequently, the number of parameters required to define this distribution can be significantly reduced compared to traditional methods. Simulation results demonstrate that this PMBM filter effectively tracks multiple airborne targets, and its performance aligns closely with an idealized panoptic baseline. These findings confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach, offering a practical solution for air traffic administration systems. Potential applications also extend to scenarios involving multiple acoustic sources and other similar contexts. Soccer managers frequently face difficult decisions regarding substitutions, particularly in late-stage critical situations. Although these moments are high-pressure, they often lack the time complexity required by algorithms commonly used in games like chess or Go. To address this, we introduce a novel approach combining a graph neural network (GNN) for feature extraction and an actor-critic method from reinforcement learning to optimize substitution strategies. Designed to operate entirely offline, the model learns a policy by simulating matches and evaluating their outcomes. Using a dataset of over 38,000 games from the German Bundesliga between the 2017/2018 and 2019/2020 seasons, our results demonstrate that an agent trained on this policy can achieve an average of 1.7 additional goals per game compared to baseline methods. When applied to real-world scenarios, the proposed strategy aligns closely with actual managerial actions in similar contexts, though it often recommends earlier substitutions in certain situations. Further analysis reveals that match context significantly influences optimal policies, and the agent successfully identifies non-obvious opportunities to improve team performance through tactical adjustments. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanElshafie/GNN-AC-Soccer.

We introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of machine common sense knowledge structured as a collection of if-then reasoning traces. This resource serves as a vital reference for both human and automated systems developing natural language representations of common knowledge. Distinct from prior knowledge graphs that primarily link entities or concepts, ATOMIC explicitly models events and the actions causing them within natural language. Consequently, it functions as a vital toolkit for training AI systems on inferential reasoning over common sense. To facilitate the generation and consumption of these reasoning traces, we outline necessary capabilities for natural language systems and provide corresponding implementations in both neural and symbolic approaches. This paper introduces a novel method for point-wise video forecasting that leverages a dual representation to more effectively model long-term video dynamics. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on recurrent or convolutional layers to capture temporal dependencies, our method's first representation learns global contextual dependencies through attention mechanisms. The second representation then models local temporal dependencies via a convolutional layer. We provide theoretical evidence demonstrating that this dual representation framework requires fewer samples to learn than conventional methods. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets confirm that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art video forecasting models. The source code is available at https://github.com/Meiram/DRNet.

The metric dimension of a graph $G$ represents the dimension required to uniquely locate any vertex using shortest path distances from an optimal set of resolved vertices, as measured by the metric dimension function $md(G)). This study examines the minimum number of vertices necessary for a graph of diameter at most $d$ to achieve a metric dimension of at least $k$, denoted as $n_0(G)$. We investigate this metric dimension under the standard path metric and also define and analyze it via an alternative metric $d_1$, which counts the maximum number of edges (with multiplicity) on a shortest path between pairs of vertices. We establish upper bounds for $n_0(G)$ under both $d$ and $d_1$, demonstrating that these bounds are tight for specific graph types. Additionally, we determine the exact values of $n_0(G)$ for certain families of trees and unicyclic graphs. Our findings have implications for identifying the minimum degree of graphs within specified diameter constraints that satisfy particular metric properties. These results are relevant to networking, specifically concerning the minimum degree required for topologies with limited diameter, and to biology, especially in protein folding regarding chains with a fixed number of hydrogen bonds. Our analysis relies on a simplified method for calculating the metric dimension that utilizes a special tree-like structure called a resolution forest, which serves as a path metric analogue to a resolving forest in graph theory. This approach offers a simpler alternative to the traditional method, which involves constructing a resolving matrix and determining the linear independence of its rows. We conclude by outlining how to adapt this technique for the injective metric dimension. This work also introduces the concept of the metric dimension under the $1$-arc metric and defines a corresponding injective metric dimension under this same metric.

The rapid global dissemination of the novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) has triggered extensive efforts to characterize its transmission dynamics through contact tracing, statistical modeling, and theoretical frameworks. While significant progress has been made in developing models to guide public health strategies and evaluate interventions, there remains a pressing need to enhance our understanding of viral spread and the efficacy of measures like lockdowns and social distancing. This article provides an overview of various mathematical approaches used to describe SARS-CoV-2 outbreaks, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations. We specifically examine how these models can be leveraged to derive key epidemiological metrics, assess the impact of control actions, and trace infection pathways. Additionally, we introduce a unified framework designed to compare different modeling strategies and their outputs. It is crucial to recognize that no single model perfectly captures all aspects of disease transmission; rather, the selection of an appropriate framework depends on the specific research objectives, available data, and intended applications. Ultimately, the utility of any model is defined by its capacity to address the unique epidemiological challenges posed by the SARS-CoV-2 outbreak. This perspective piece does not establish a hierarchical ranking of models but serves to illustrate the diversity of methodologies employed to analyze the current epidemic. By synthesizing these approaches, we aim to clarify their uses and potential, offering guidance for future research during this crisis and beyond. Complementing this review, a collection of 24 associated articles explores specific mathematical models and their roles in investigating the SARS-CoV-2 outbreak.

We present the first detailed investigation into Bussola's proposed $log(M*)$-$SFR$ relation (R1), which differs from the standard relation by its double-power law shape. While Bussola's curve aligns well with observed data points, the underlying slope at specific intervals remains steep enough that minor shifts in the distribution of points can significantly alter the apparent fit. When compared against a broad range of selected tracer-based $M*$ spectra from literature, R1 fits generally perform worse than both the standard relation and a simple double power law. Furthermore, the double power law requires a breaking mass at least as high as $10^{11} M_{\odot}$, contrasting with R1's breaking point of $\sim 10^{10.2} M_{\odot}$. Notably, when analyzing the most common measurement method for massive galaxies—where bulge dominance is difficult to detect—R1 provides an excellent fit. This suggests that the traditional view attributing the turnover in the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses to the increasing bulge fraction in central galaxies may be incorrect. Instead, our findings indicate that the slope of the MS at the turn-over in Bussola's relation is roughly twice as steep as previously thought necessary, implying that the dominant factor driving the turnover at high masses is likely a physical mechanism rather than a change in galaxy structure. We conclude by discussing the potential implications of these results. (This work was originally titled: Does Bussola's $log(M*)$-SFR Relation Reveal a Different Measurement Bias for Star Formation Rates in Massive Galaxies?).

Fake news spreads rapidly across social media, posing significant dangers by misleading the public and undermining trust in media outlets. While deep fakes present challenges in combating image-based false content, text-based misinformation remains a persistent issue that is difficult to address using methods effective against visual fake news. This problem is particularly acute for automated detection systems, which often fail to recognize creative linguistic framing designed to evade classification. Furthermore, existing approaches have been limited by reliance on Eurocentric datasets and the scarcity of multilingual data required to train and deploy deep learning models. We introduce a few-shot learning framework capable of identifying false news in multiple languages without requiring large-scale dataset training. By leveraging both image and text modalities from fact-checked datasets, our meta-learning model generates vector representations of verified articles to classify new, unseen pieces as either real or fake. Notably, this system functions effectively even when provided with access to a specific fact-checking organization's database rather than a broad, diverse dataset. Evaluations conducted across three widely used datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions. The source code and a survey of relevant literature are available at https://github.com/Anusha0709/METAFACT. Multilingual few-shot learning, meta learning, and fraud detection remain active areas of research with substantial potential for future development.

Feature extraction serves as a vital preprocessing technique in unsupervised learning tasks. Recently, embedding layers derived from comparative learning have been applied to specific problems, such as one-shot classification. However, a comprehensive study exploring feature extraction through comparative learning remains absent. This work introduces an unsupervised method grounded in comparative learning, offering a straightforward and effective approach for embedding data into low-dimensional spaces. The proposed technique, termed UniFEC (Unified Structure for Feature Extraction based on Comparative Learning), functions as a universal framework capable of accommodating various feature engineering methods, including histogram-based, hand-crafted features, and pre-trained dictionary features (for instance, BERT and GloVe). UniFEC enables the integration and joint learning of diverse feature types within a task. Its efficacy is validated across three natural language processing tasks: sentiment analysis, question answering, and text classification. The utility of this framework is further demonstrated by applying UniFEC to a low-resource language, Burmese, to enhance the performance of state-of-the-art models. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChinHuiYoon/UniFEC. Large language models (LLMs) possess extensive world knowledge encoded as statistical patterns, enabling them to answer queries about factual events, entities, and phenomena without direct experience. This capability can be enhanced by integrating structured knowledge graphs (KGs), which offer precise, symbolic representations of facts. While recent methods like T5-LLM, PaLM-LLM, and MetaLLM attempt to combine KGs and LLMs by converting graph nodes and edges into text for retrieval-augmented generation, these approaches often fail to preserve the semantic richness of the structured data. Similarly, techniques that utilize natural language templates to query a knowledge graph before feeding results to an LLM for responses risk losing information during the final output stage. To address these limitations, we introduce the Ability framework, a novel system that leverages a knowledge graph's semantic metadata to guide an LLM in processing and incorporating that metadata into conversations. Through human evaluations, our framework significantly outperformed baseline methods—specifically T5-LLM, PaLM-LLM, MetaLLM, and a baseline utilizing NL-oriented metadata—across three distinct knowledge graph datasets in terms of answer quality, reasoning accuracy, and overall effectiveness. The source code and dataset required for reproduction are accessible at https://github.com/Aniruddha-1/Ability.

It is well established that a minimal immersion into $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is always biharmonic; conversely, in dimensions three and higher, no compact biharmonic hypersurfaces without mean curvature exist within this space. We demonstrate that if an umbilic point at a boundary between distinct recurrent operator regions occurs, the hypersurface must be minimal. Under specific conditions, we prove that a biharmonic hypersurface with mean curvature $H$ (where $H$ is sufficiently small) and exactly one recurrent operator region (excluding the negative identity) in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ ($n\geq 3$) cannot be immersed as a rotationally symmetric MMCH (mixed mean curvature hyper surface). Finally, we provide a classification of biharmonic hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ that possess precisely two distinct recurrent operators.

We investigate the acoustic emissions generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant pulling velocity, as recorded using a laser vibrometer and a condenser microphone. The resulting sound profile displays a sequence of transient bursts separated by quieter intervals. By converting the audio into a time-frequency representation via short-time Fourier transform, we identified distinct circular patterns superimposed on the burst segments, indicative of crackling caused by slippage between specific frequency bands. Analysis of both the time-domain signal and the spectrogram reveals that the dominant frequencies within each burst increase linearly with the tape's unwinding speed. When the sound is played back, these bursts manifest as clicks followed by creases; consequently, the spectrogram's circular structures appear as concentric rings. Upon plotting the activity of sliding bands in the spectrogram's time-row, clear ordered patterns emerge, likely resulting from the tape's rotation within the sound spectrogram. Furthermore, constructing a sound spectrogram on logarithmic frequencies uncovers additional hidden patterns, suggesting the presence of further ordered structures within the acoustic data. These regularities are visually confirmed by creating a "spectrogram of a spectrogram" on linearly scaled frequencies. Finally, we propose a simple mechanical model to account for the coexistence of these different sliding band patterns when displayed on a conventional versus a logarithmically scaled spectrogram.

Deriving unsupervised semantic representations from raw point clouds remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a framework that integrates a hybrid regularization strategy with a novel data transformation, termed transformation-unique (TU), to enhance the learning of semantic classifications for point clouds. We establish the theoretical foundations for both the unique (U) and unique in distribution (UDIn) properties of the TU transformation. Furthermore, we introduce a network architecture incorporating a layer dedicated to the TU transformation to classify new data. The proposed framework, named PointCloud-Unique (TPC), is evaluated against state-of-the-art methods using three standard datasets: ShapeNetPart, ModelNet10, and ModelNet40. Assessment criteria include the classification accuracy for unseen parts or shapes on these datasets and a comparison of regularization strategies. Our results demonstrate that the combination of unique (U) properties with shape-part semantics effectively boosts accuracy. The source code for TPC is accessible at: https://github.com/rajivkumar1992/PointCloud-Unique.

Effective feedback mechanisms are essential for enhancing the quality of both compiled code and source programs. Our geometric framework unifies semantic and syntactic aspects to enable effective end-to-end optimization and verification. This framework introduces a quantitative metric for the distance between program fragments, facilitating the identification of optimal syntactic alignments between compiled and source representations to support feedback-driven optimization. Additionally, it provides a framework for feedback-directed refinement types, offering a method to computationally derive simple type-directed suggestions for complex interventional effects. We demonstrate the utility of this framework through two applications: connecting cross-compilation feedback with iteratively explicit feedback for syntactic interventions, and linking interventional refinement types with nominal types for improved error reporting. These applications highlight how a single metric can serve multiple purposes, such as optimizing feedback sources and improving error messages, and how different interventions can be composed. The framework is implemented in CompElle, an extension of Celle, a compiler for the Elaborate language, which builds upon the OCaml base. Implementation details and further applications are discussed elsewhere.

This paper presents a proof of the $l$-adic local Langlands correspondence for characters of the absolute Galois group attached to an inertial prime $p$, extending the result by Breuil and Méndez (2019) to a broader context. Additionally, we establish a reciprocity law linking the existence of Hecke eigenvalues for GL_2 to the congruences between Eisenstein and Carmichael lifts of Serre weights, generalizing the classical congruence between Serre and Deligne-Lusztig weights. These findings are expected to facilitate the investigation of Serre's reciprocity law, which connects the parameters of two Lifts of the "Serre Weight" $D$ via the congruences of their $t$- and $a$-invariants. A byproduct of our approach is the derivation of explicit formulas for the cohomological invariant $a$ of a Serre Weight $D$ (at a specific inertial prime $p$) from its character $\rho$, utilizing the theory of automorphic representations of PGL_2 over $\mathbb{Q}$ and its related "main component group". The methods employed here are purely Galois-theoretic and rely on Kummer theory, offering an alternative to the combination of Ribet's techniques and the explicit class field theory utilized in the work of Breuil and Méndez. Consequently, these approaches could potentially be applied in other contexts where Ribet's methods and explicit class field theory are relevant.

This study introduces a method to precisely determine damage initiation in self-sensing composite laminates via electrical impedance tomography ( Zit ). While Zit offers high sensitivity for detecting and localizing damage, it struggles with exact identification once cracking begins. To address this, a hybrid approach combines Zit with a genetic algorithm ( Ga ) for post-processing data. First, the technique's sensitivity is validated through numerical experiments on a simple two-ply laminate with a 90° delamination, comparing results against known artificial defects. Second, the method is applied experimentally to a complex laminate to detect and locate an intentional delamination, with accuracy confirmed by sectioning. Finally, the protocol is used in real-time to identify an unexpected delamination caused by impact, successfully pinpointing the event within 20 ms. This non-contact, real-time, point-source-based protocol requires no prior assumptions about defect shape, size, or number. Additionally, the exact localization enabled by this method provides a step-wise analysis of delamination growth under progressive loading, offering valuable insights for damage management. The resulting Zit/Ga strategy serves as an effective real-time protocol for quality control and damage control in composites, potentially reducing the reliance on costly destructive testing. Furthermore, this method pairs well with surrogate modeling techniques, such as the exact delamination modeling proposed in reference [ 1 ], to create optimized damage control systems. This combination opens new possibilities for active damage control using shape memory alloy wires or self-healing agents to mitigate delamination. Ultimately, this complete workflow—from real-time localization via Zit/Ga to optimal control using exact models—constitutes a novel, end-to-end solution for delamination management in composites. Elevated order methods, first introduced by Burda and Sorensen in 1991, offer a technique to accelerate matrix inversions by trading increased computational complexity per iteration for fewer required iterations to reach a target accuracy. This paper generalizes that second-order approach to an n-th order method and implements it on a GPU. When inverted an 11,000 \times 11,000 density matrix to an accuracy of 10−9, the second-order method completed the task in 10 seconds, whereas the traditional direct inversion took approximately 20 minutes. The generalized n-th order method achieved even faster convergence; reaching the same accuracy in just under a second, it demonstrated that doubling the order further reduces processing time. Once the matrix is initially inverted to an approximate accuracy (which determines the final computation's precision), the n-th order method can refine it to any desired level of accuracy efficiently. The goal is to minimize regret by leveraging a teacher's losses, which consist of a linear loss over the context features plus noise. This learning takes place across a network of agents, each with its own local feature vector, under the constraint that contexts remain private. The agent must learn a strategy to select actions using only local features and the statistical distribution of contexts at each node, all while assuming linear optimal play. We developed a 3D global hydrodynamical simulation to investigate how dust development influences the excitation and growth of the VSI (vertical shear instability) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Our results indicate that while gas molecular weights remain uniform in regions without dust, the accumulation of solid particles creates radial variations. These variations cause vertical shear flows to generate turbulent motions that erode dust layers, thereby limiting dust concentration and preventing the formation of distinct dust bands. Furthermore, we found that such erosion suppresses VSI-driven turbulence, as measured by the Rossby number, within the dust layer itself. However, strong vertical shear persists outside this layer, where gas molecular weight is uniform, sustaining turbulent activity. We observe that dust settling enhances this external turbulence, with the Rossby number rising by factors of 2 to 4 compared to simulations lacking dust development. These outcomes suggest that dust settling and radial diffusion are interdependent processes that can occur more efficiently than previously thought, potentially aiding the formation of large, low-density dust structures required for gravitational instability. Additionally, our data reveal that VSI turbulence is significantly stronger in the outer disk zones than in their corresponding inner regions. Consistency regularization represents a prominent approach in semi-supervised learning, where the network is trained to generate identical predictions for different data augmentations of the same input. While effective, implementing this strategy often presents significant challenges, particularly when utilizing high-dimensional pixel-wise labels in medical image segmentation. This paper introduces a novel consistency regularization method that effectively addresses these difficulties. The proposed technique leverages a recently developed framework for semantic matching between structured data sets, known as "awkward" regularization. We integrate this with consistency regularization to create a hybrid method. When combined with mean teachers, this approach yields "awkwardly simple" consistency regularization. We validate the effectiveness of this method across two medical image segmentation tasks using publicly available datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods, requiring only minimal hyperparameter tuning. Furthermore, we establish the theoretical soundness of this method by proving that "awkward" regularization effectively leverages label information from both supervised and unsupervised datasets. Additionally, we provide theoretical evidence that the integration of consistency regularization with feature-level label smoothing—achieved here through awkward regularization—enhances the network's ability to classify unseen classes during inference, a characteristic that has not been explicitly guaranteed in prior consistency regularization frameworks. As with consistency regularization, this benefit is particularly advantageous for segmenting foreground objects that appear infrequently in the training data. Ultimately, this work presents an accessible consistency regularization framework suitable for various semi-supervised learning applications involving structured data. We illustrate its utility for medical image segmentation and highlight its potential for other tasks where predictions must be made among a fixed set of categories, for which consistency regularization can offer specific advantages. Hypothesis testing serves as a fundamental method for evaluating scientific claims, with p-values and Bayes factors representing the two primary statistical approaches. While the integration of Bayes factors with replication constitutes a standard framework for the scientific method, its practical application has been limited by the labor-intensive nature of traditional workflows. This paper re-examines the principles of Bayes factors and replication to develop more efficient strategies for their computation. These optimized workflows enable the deeply repeated use of Bayes factors within a Bayesian analysis, a technique that has historically been advocated as a more rigorous alternative to the repeatedly applied p-values commonly found in data dredging or fishing expeditions. Although such extensive Bayesian analyses are computationally demanding, the resulting posterior distribution of Bayes factors offers a superior metric for assessing the strength of evidence compared to the distribution of Cp-values (the complement of p-values). Furthermore, the study revisits the debate between subjective and objective Bayesianism, demonstrating how an empirical distribution of Bayes factors can facilitate the determination of hyperpriors for Bayes factors in a fully objective Bayesian framework. The research concludes by applying these workflow strategies to a real-world scenario involving the search for new physics beyond the standard model at the Large Hadron Collider. Key terms include: Bayes factor, hypothesis testing, new physics, Large Hadron Collider, and objective Bayesianism.

We demonstrate an atomic interferometric experiment designed to detect local magnetic field variations caused by the Meissner effect and magnetic flux trapping during the cooling of a superconducting lead (Pb) disk. Initially, we characterize linear magnetic field sensitivities of two atomic interferometers—configured as Mach-Zehnder and Kagnor-Sagnac paths—within the vicinity of the Pb disk. Subsequently, we detail the method for measuring the supercurrent flowing through the disk via the local magnetic field changes induced by the Meissner effect and flux trapping during the cooling process. Finally, we report a precise determination of the enclosed supercurrent and its standard uncertainty as $I_{s}=1.37(\pm 0.02)$ mA. This accuracy represents a significant improvement over previous measurements, achieved by leveraging the high precision of atomic interferometry to indirectly detect the supercurrent. This study confirms that atomic interferometry can effectively detect extremely weak magnetic fields, such as those arising from the Meissner effect and flux trapping, to precisely quantify the enclosed supercurrent in a superconductor. Verifying this capability is vital for developing magnetometers based on the magnetic Aharonov-Bohm effect for sensitive detection of the Josephson current in SPS junctions. To this end, we sensitively measured local field changes from a Josephson effect lead (Pb) disk using an atomic interferometric setup, successfully determining its critical current with an uncertainty of $I_{c}=1.35(\pm 0.02)$ mA, validating the feasibility of this approach. These findings indicate that atomic interferometry can precisely determine the critical current in a superconducting disk by sensitively detecting local magnetic field alterations resulting from the Josephson effect. This study introduces the formulation of Cauchy principles and Euler equations within the initial principles framework of magnetic materials, specifically tailored for the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) state system. We establish both classical and relativistic Eulerian initial principles theories for YSR states, complementing the existing Lagrangian approach. The relativistic initial principles theory of YSR states offers a coordinate and material frame invariant framework, capable of calculating higher-order responses of YSR states to electromagnetic fields, thereby enabling the determination of magneto-optical effects. We apply the classical relativistic initial principles theory to analyze recent experiments on an Mn adatom and Mn dimers on Nb(110), predicting a magneto-optical Kerr effect. Furthermore, we anticipate that the relativistic initial principles theory of YSR states will facilitate the investigation of other superconducting magnetic systems through future experimental studies. Finally, we conclude that this theory will serve as a robust theoretical framework for examining quantum phenomena such as the YSR state and Andreev bound states. Key expressions for the one-body current density and spin density operators required for this research are collected in an appendix. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that the initial principles theories of superconducting magnetic materials can be developed via the continuum mechanics approach, analogous to the establishment of such theories for conventional magnetic materials. Our findings indicate that the relativistic initial principles theory of YSR states will function as a comprehensive framework, facilitating the exploration of various quantum effects in superconducting magnetic materials, including the YSR state, Andreev bound states, Josephson currents, and magneto-optical phenomena. Such a theory will also support the development of a relativistic initial currents finite element method for modeling electromagnetic, spin, and Josephson currents in these materials. Additionally, this research confirms that the concepts of Lagrangian, Eulerian, and initial frames and their corresponding coordinates are applicable to the YSR state system. We anticipate that these findings will guide future investigations into wave mechanics, initial principles theories, and continuum theories of the YSR state and related superconducting magnetic systems. This work serves as the first report on the development of initial principles theories for the YSR state system. Dermatologists face significant challenges in accurately classifying skin lesions due to the vast and complex dataset required for effective image recognition systems. Introducing a novel approach, this study employs Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) to identify various skin cancers from dermoscopic images. Building on the Wide Residual Network (WRN) architecture, we integrated a post-CNN module designed to detect and exclude outliers—images that do not fit standard dermatological categories—utilizing an entropy-based method. Experimental results demonstrate that the modified WRN-28 architecture achieved an accuracy of 99.55%, surpassing the performance of other models on the dataset. Furthermore, when applied to a real-world clinical dataset, the model achieved an accuracy of 87.14%. These findings indicate that the proposed framework effectively handles both standard and real-world dermatological datasets, offering a valuable tool for aiding medical professionals in diagnosis. At the core of this project lies a novel formulation of the Godel sentence that incorporates a specific predicate from the Tarski hierarchy. This new version, referred to as the Godel-Tarski sentence, yields a shorter proof of the first-order unprovability of the Tarski sentence compared to the standard Godel sentence. Furthermore, we introduce a family of predicates generalizing the Godel-Tarski sentence, called the Rosser-Tarski predicates, which enable us to establish a family of sentences that prove the unprovability of the $n$-th predicate of the Tarski hierarchy for each $n>1$. These results are achieved using a diagonalization operator defined over the Godel-Tarsni and Rosser-Tarski predicates, an operator that generalizes the usual Godel numbering operator. Additionally, we define a diagonalization operator over the Tarski predicates themselves to prove a related unprovability result. Finally, we provide proofs of several of these sentences via an outer model argument, an approach that allows for more significant iterations of the Rosser sentence than previously possible with the Godel-Tarsni or Rosser-Tarsni sentences alone. The proofs of these diagonalization and unprovability results rely on a new characterization of the set of true sentences in a countable model of $\mathbf{ZFC}$ with respect to the Godel, Godel-Tarsni, and Tarski predicates.

Invariant manifolds, including curves and surfaces, play a crucial role in the qualitative analysis of dynamical systems near nonhyperbolic fixed points. This study examines the feasibility of constructing invariant surfaces for fractional-order systems. We demonstrate that certain irrational surfaces satisfy the invariance condition for a specific class of linear fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we prove that no irrational smooth invariant surface exists for a particular system of coupled Riccati equations with a specific order combination. Additionally, we show that irrational smooth invariant surfaces cannot exist for some systems of Bogoliubov equations. These findings indicate that invariant surfaces are generally restricted to rational orders, a characteristic that can be leveraged to identify and eliminate spurious solutions in numerical simulations of fractional-order systems. Leveraging these results, we derive the first global linearization theorem for a system of Caputo fractional-order Lorenz equations. As an application of our main findings, we utilize a topological conjugation method to establish the existence of a family of homoclinic orbits connecting the origin to the line of equilibrium points for a system of Atangana-Baleanu fractional-order Lorenz equations. Consequently, we conclude that the classical topological theory of dynamical systems remains effective for certain systems of coupled fractional-order differential equations. Regarding the specific system under consideration, we correct an error in a recent publication concerning the stability of a heteroclinic cycle, providing the correct form of this cycle. Finally, we correct another mistake related to a heteroclinic connection involving a pair of Hopf cycles from the same source, offering the appropriate description for this structure. As a byproduct of this correction, we introduce and analyze a new configuration of invariant sets: a figure-eight shaped heteroclinic orbit linking two pairs of Hopf cycles. This shape represents a novel geometric structure of invariant sets within the phase space for this system of fractional-order differential equations. To achieve these results, we employ a combination of techniques from operator theory, topology, and the classical topological theory of dynamical systems. This study investigates the inverse issue of determining initial conditions from final ones within a structural acoustic system. The goal is to recover initial interface deformations and velocities, as well as initial acoustic pressures, using final boundary measurements of the acoustic field. Under specific assumptions regarding interface deformations, the problem is shown to be both uniquely solvable and capable of stable reconstruction of the initial states. To address this, a global optimization method based on gradient descent is implemented. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively recovers initial interface deformations and velocities, as well as acoustic pressures, from boundary data. These results confirm the method's utility for identifying missing initial conditions in similar systems and highlight its potential as a non-invasive technique for assessing damage in engineering structures. Furthermore, this global optimization framework offers a universal framework for solving other ill-posed inverse problems in structural acoustic systems. Finally, to utilize this method in practical applications, a faster alternative to the global optimization approach is required. Developing such an efficient algorithm remains the focus of future research. (This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant 11971355.)

This spectrum comprises a single scalar singlet $\eta$ and the smallest possible number of right-handed neutrons necessary to establish the seesaw mechanism.
